messages.subject: [statnet_help] applying ERGM to a word co-occurrence network
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] applying ERGM to a word co-occurrence network
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone!

As part of my master degree in statistics I'm writing a work on Network
Analysis and it requires a practical application of the analysis of a real
network.

The network in question is a co-occurrence network of words, obtained from
a collection of tweets regarding the food industry. The result is a
weighted undirected network of 346 nodes and 2123 edges where the weights
are the jaccard indexes (a standardized index of co-occurrence) between
words, but I used a cut-off to make it binary and keep things as simple as
possible. I also have some additional node attributes like word topic, word
type(noun, verb, etc) and word total frequency.

The objective of the analysis should be finding useful commercial insights
for a particular food brand.

As much as I searched I couldn't find much about this particular type of
network, except some articles about them used as visual rapresentation of
text, and the recognition of central concepts using betweenes centrality.

I'd like to put in the work an application of ERGM, but I have some doubts:

-First of all, I'm not really sure if ERGMs are useful or even viable for
this particular network type, this doubt coming from the fact that I
couldn't find anything about the modeling of such networks, and I can't
tell if it's because infeasibility, because no one ever tried or because
the natural language processing methods are much better for this
environment.

-If the application of ERGMs in this setting is viable, do you have any
suggestion regarding the terms to include? For a start I decided to include
the nodemix term for the topic (using only the interesting matches). I know
it's a decision that depends on the exact network arrangement, but any
generic advice is welcome.

I'm sorry in advance if this message is somewhat off-topic, not regarding
the statnet suite directly.

Goodbye and thanks for any advice,

Michael Rossero

messages.subject: [statnet_help] applying ERGM to a word co-occurrence network
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] applying ERGM to a word co-occurrence network
messages.body_plain:
Hi Michael,

The short answer is that ERGMs may be relevant, but it depends on your 
research question.

One of Mark Handcock's students used ERGMs for language analysis -- Danny 
Wyatt.  You can find some of his work from google scholar: 
http://scholar.google.com/citations?user=q9UyGCIAAAAJ&hl=en

The new weighted versions of ERGMs could be used for the original weighted 
networks, but weighted networks require (quite) a bit more thought than 
binary.  We have a tutorial up on the statnet website:

https://statnet.csde.washington.edu/trac/attachment/wiki/Sunbelt2013/Valued.pdf

For the binary network you describe, you can put in a nodemix term, but 
the question is what attributes should govern the mixing.  I'm assuming 
it's not just nouns vs. verbs.  If you were really interested in 
co-occurrence of specific words, then the attribute to mix on is node ID, 
but that would require 346x345/2 = 59K+ parameters, so I don't think you 
want to do that.

In short, ERGMs are potentially useful here, but you would need to specify 
a theoretical model first, and then assess the feasibility.

You might also consider an MDS approach on the original weighted network 
if you want to identify word "neighborhoods".  The "latentnet" package in 
statnet provides an alternative approach to this kind of latent space 
modeling.  Pavel will be teaching a workshop on latentnet at the Sunbelt 
this year.

HTH,
Martina

 However, whenever I try to do anything with my attributes, it will not

9#######. I have over 800 respondents.)  I should note that the adjacency

messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] fitting ergms to data from link-tracing designs
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Michal. The current version of ergm() will, when given a network 
with missing edges, find the observed-data MLE under the assumption that 
the observed data is ignorably sampled from the graph being modeled. H+G 
discuss the conditions under which that is a reasonable assumption...but 
where it is, ergm() should work out of the box.

An alternative approach (closer to what is in the tutorial you mention) 
is to obtain an approximate MLE by (1) using design-based estimation to 
obtain (approximate) sufficient statistics, and (2) fitting to those 
target stats (using the functionality currently in ERGM). Note that to 
do this in a valid manner, the graph used for simulation in ERGM must be 
of the same size as the graph from which your data was sampled -- this 
means that the method does not scale so well if one has a really large 
system (e.g., an OSN). One advantage of this approach is that it makes 
it easier to relax the assumption that the seed nodes for the link-trace 
were drawn from a probability sample (by using Markov chain-based 
sampling methods - see, e.g., Gjoka et al., IEEE JSAC, 2011). (Of 
course, that only helps you if you are in a position to choose your data 
collection design!) If your design-based estimators are consistent, then 
the associated approximate MLE should be consistent as well, but your 
measures of standard error will in general be underestimated (because 
they neglect the sampling variability in your estimates of the 
sufficient statistics). My impression is that Pavel is currently working 
on this (or, if not, a closely related problem!).

Mark or others may want to chime in on this, but that should at least 
give you the basic rundown....

-Carter

messages.subject: [statnet_help] GOF with missing edges
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] GOF with missing edges
messages.body_plain:
Hi Julija,

On 1/27/2014 2:31 AM, Julija Mell wrote:
>
> Hi all,
>
> I have a question about evaluating goodness of fit with missing data:
>
> I have a network with missing edges on which I fit an ergm model. When 
> I then proceed to gof -- how does gof treat the NAs in my network? 
> When I run gof(model) it seems that NAs are interpreted as 0s -- e.g. 
> non-respondents seem to be considered as isolates: the "observed" 
> statistics have a lot of degree-0's and infinite geodesic distances. 
> This doesn't seem to be right.
>
Indeed, this is the case: calculation for many of the summary statistics 
entails NAs being interpreted as 0s.  The documentation for the sna 
package (whose routines often lie behind other functions) provides some 
guidance about this.  There is some discussion about whether we ought to 
be returning NAs when someone attempts to calculate a statistic on a 
network when that network contains NAs instead of treating them as 0s.  
Thoughts form users welcome here.

In general, the missing data capabilities are not fully developed, and 
even knowing what it would mean to handle missing data is hard to define 
in some cases.  In the case of gof, for instance, we typically want to 
compare networks simulated from a model to the observed network on a 
number of network statistics.  If there's missing data in the observed 
network, then probably the fairest comparison for the simulated networks 
is to the observed network with its missing values imputed from the 
model.  Note that while this is not currently built into gof, it's 
something you can try to do on your own, and I think were headed in that 
direction with your subsequent code:
>
> I have also tried running gof(model,constraints=~observed) but then I 
> consistently receive the following error:
>
> > test2<-gof(mfit,verbose=T,constraints=~observed)
>
> Starting GOF for the given ERGM formula.
>
> Calculating observed network statistics.
>
> Starting simulations.
>
> Sim 1 of 100 : Starting MCMC iterations to generate 1 network
>
> Sampler accepted  46.970% of 10000 proposed steps.
>
> Finished simulation 1 of 1.
>
> Sim 2 of 100 :
>
> Error in InitMHP.randomtoggleNonObserved(list(constraints = 
> list(observed = list( :
>
>   The passed network does not have any non-observed dyads.
>
> Hence constraining to the observed will hold the network fixed at this 
> network.
>
> Either the network or the constraint need to be altered.
>
Yes, this constraint won't work with the gof command.  Note that it 
worked on the first simulation, because that one was simulated from the 
observed network, which contains missing data.  But then the second 
simulated network is simulated off the first simulated network, which 
doesn't contain missing data.  Instead, try using this same constraint 
with the simulate command instead of gof. Make sure to set the argument 
sequential=FALSE, so that each network will be simulated off the base.  
This will give you a bunch of networks in which the missing data are 
imputed.You can then do simulate without the constraint to simulate a 
bunch of new networks from the underlying model.  Then, you can write 
your own code to calculate the statistics you want to compare on the two 
sets, and then compare them numerically or graphically.  These last 
steps are what gof does automatically, but here you'll have to do it by 
hand because of having a set of imputed "observed" networks instead of 
just a single observed network.

Making some wrapper functions to make all this happen behind the scenes 
is something we can consider doing, but in the meantime, you should be 
able to make progress on your work this way.

There might also be other similar comparisons of interest here that I 
haven't thought of.  If others have ideas, please chime in!

HTH,
Steve



> Thanks for any help with regard to how to deal with gof and missing edges!
>
> Best,
>
> Julija

So you have a binomial distribution then, and a simple binomial test of 
whether p=0.5.  There are lots of calculators online to do that, just 
google "binomial test".  Given your bipartite data, the independence 
assumption you need to make is that the status of one edge for a node does 
not influence the status of another edge for that node, or for any other 
node.  The legitimacy of that assumption depends on your substantive 
theory.

hth,
Martina
